introduction: This intermediate tier drives into the maxims that dictate civil liability, the Law of Torts, and equitable remedies. These phrases determine who pays compensation and when a right actually translates into a legal remedy.

core_concepts.title: Ubi jus ibi remedium
core_concepts.description:
Meaning: 'Where there is a right, there is a remedy'.
- Application: The cornerstone of the Law of Torts (established in the classic *Ashby v. White* case regarding the right to vote). It signifies that if the law confers a right upon a person, it must also provide a mechanism (remedy) to vindicate that right if it is violated.

core_concepts.title: Volenti non fit injuria
core_concepts.description:
Meaning: 'To a willing person, no injury is done'.
- Application: A major defense in Torts. If a person voluntarily consents to take a risk, they cannot later sue if they suffer harm (e.g., A spectator hit by a ball at a cricket match cannot sue the stadium). The consent must be free and informed.

core_concepts.title: Res ipsa loquitur
core_concepts.description:
Meaning: 'The thing speaks for itself'.
- Application: A rule of evidence used in Negligence cases. Normally, the plaintiff must prove the defendant was negligent. However, under this maxim, if an accident occurs that *could not possibly have happened without negligence* (e.g., a surgical sponge left inside a patient's body), the burden of proof shifts to the defendant to prove they were NOT negligent.

core_concepts.title: Quid pro quo
core_concepts.description:
Meaning: 'Something for something'.
- Application: The basis of 'Consideration' in Contract Law. A valid contract requires mutual exchange of value; one party gives something to get something in return.

core_concepts.title: Nemo dat quod non habet
core_concepts.description:
Meaning: 'No one can give what he does not have'.
- Application: A fundamental rule of property and sales law (Sale of Goods Act, Section 27). A person cannot transfer a better title to property than they themselves possess. (If a thief sells you a stolen laptop, you do not become the legal owner, because the thief had no legal title to give).

important_entities.name: Damnum sine injuria & Injuria sine damno
important_entities.significance: *Damnum sine injuria*: Damage without legal injury (e.g., A rival shop opens next to yours causing you financial loss. No lawsuit is possible because no legal right was violated). *Injuria sine damno*: Legal injury without actual damage (e.g., Trespassing on your land without causing harm. Lawsuit IS possible because the legal right to exclusive possession was violated).

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: Does *Volenti non fit injuria* apply if someone is injured while trying to rescue another person? **NO**. The 'Rescue Cases' doctrine dictates that if someone acts under a moral or legal compulsion to save a life endangered by the defendant's negligence, the defense of *Volenti* fails. The rescuer CAN sue the negligent party.

mnemonics_and_tricks.memory_phrase: Injuria = Injury to Right. If Injuria is present, you win. If Injuria is absent (Sine Injuria), you lose.
mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: Always look for the word 'Injuria' to determine if a tort case is actionable.

exam_strategy_tips: If a CLAT PG question asks about the legal principle behind shifting the burden of proof in obvious medical negligence cases, select **Res ipsa loquitur**.
